# Why people play: motivators and example games

This note collects what the main frameworks of player motivation say about
why people play, and which games each source gives as examples. It draws on
the course books, the papers behind each framework, and industry surveys
from 2021 and 2025. Every source is listed in full in the bibliography at
the end, so you can find it and check any claim yourself.

**How to read the citations.** A citation gives author and year, and the
bibliography is alphabetical by author within each group. Page numbers
follow the edition the bibliography lists. *Rules of Play* and *Reality Is
Broken* circulate in print and ebook layouts whose page numbers differ, so
they are cited by chapter, and *Rules of Play* also by section heading;
those are the same in every copy. A game, dynamic, or mechanic appears
under a motivator only when the cited source attaches it to that motivator.
The section on attribution explains how each source chose its examples.

There is no single canonical list. Each framework carves the same territory
differently, but across the course books and the literature the motivators
settle into eleven recurring clusters. The first section takes each
motivator in turn, with the dynamics and mechanics the sources tie to it;
the rest of the note shows where each piece comes from.

## The eleven motivators

Each motivator below is described in the three layers of the MDA framework
(Hunicke et al. 2004). The **aesthetic** is what the player feels, named in
LeBlanc's terms where one exists. **Dynamics** are the patterns that emerge
while the rules run. **Mechanics** are the rules and features a designer
builds. The MDA paper draws the line between the last two with card games:
shuffling, trick-taking, and betting are mechanics, and the bluffing that
emerges from them is a dynamic (p. 4). A dynamic or mechanic is listed under
a motivator only when a cited source ties it to that motivator. Where the
sources warn that a mechanic can backfire, the warning is listed too.

### Challenge and mastery

The fiero of triumph over adversity; Koster's "learning is the drug."

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Challenge* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Bartle 1996 *Achiever*; Lazzaro 2004a *Hard Fun*; self-determination theory's *competence* (Ryan et al. 2006); Quantic Foundry *Mastery*; Koster 2013, the book's thesis (p. 40); McGonigal 2011, satisfying work and the hope of success (ch. 2); Caillois 1961 *agôn*.
- **Aesthetic:** Challenge, "game as obstacle course" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Time pressure and opponent play (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
  - Difficulty that rises as the player's ability grows (Malone 1980, p. 54) or as the player progresses through the game (Przybylski et al. 2010, p. 155).
  - The "same-but-different": a simple core mechanic that produces a new outcome each time it is played, which is how Quake can be "easy to learn but difficult to master" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Sculpting Desire").
  - Fun failure: a failure animation that makes losing enjoyable, as in Super Monkey Ball 2 (McGonigal 2011, ch. 4).
  - Levels that force the player to invent new strategies (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 2f).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Goals whose outcome is uncertain, through variable difficulty, multiple levels of goals, hidden information, or randomness (Malone 1980, pp. 66 to 67).
  - Score-keeping and speeded responses, which set goals beyond the goal (Malone 1980, p. 66).
  - Difficulty levels the player chooses, perhaps with labels like "Cadet," "Captain," and "Commander" (Malone 1980, p. 66).
  - Matchmaking on each player's history of performance, as in Halo 3 (Przybylski et al. 2010, pp. 155 to 156).
  - Controls that are "intuitive and readily mastered" (Ryan et al. 2006, p. 346).
  - Clear goals, the possibility of failure, and immediate feedback (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 2b).
  - Grades or stars on each level, which invite replay for a better mark (Schell 2019, p. 218).
  - Harsh punishment, which lets players feel proud of "having beaten such a difficult game" (Schell 2019, p. 237).
  - The highest difficulty settings, and the hardest missions and bosses (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 10).
  - Character builders and optimizing a character for its role, items in Yee's *Mechanics* subcomponent (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 11).
- **Example games:** Tetris (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1; Lazzaro 2004a); Super Monkey Ball 2, Rock Band 2 (McGonigal 2011, ch. 4); Civilization, Halo (Lazzaro 2004a); Super Mario 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (Ryan et al. 2006); Dark Souls, Super Smash Bros. Melee, XCOM, Europa Universalis (Yee 2015); Quake as "easy to learn but difficult to master" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Sculpting Desire").

### Competition over other people

- **Named by:** Bartle 1996 *Killer*; Yee 2006 *Competition*; Quantic Foundry *Competition*; Caillois 1961 *agôn*; Schell 2019, delight in another's misfortune (p. 136) and competition, the first of five reasons to play with others (p. 439).
- **Aesthetic:** MDA has no separate aesthetic for competition, though the paper lists it among Quake's aesthetics (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Adversarial play with "clear feedback about who is winning," and a winning condition every player can still believe in (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
  - Catch-up dynamics that keep trailing players in the game: subsidies for poor players and taxes on rich ones (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 4), a negative feedback loop "that punishes the lead player" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "The Role of the Goal"), or a feedback loop that keeps racers in a "dense cluster," jockeying for position (ch. 18, "Racing Loops").
  - Rivalry among friends, "one-upping each other by winning more points and prizes" (Schell 2019, p. 157).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Duels, matches, arenas, leaderboards, and rankings (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, pp. 3, 15).
  - Public high-score lists (Schell 2019, p. 232; Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 4c).
  - Both players' scores visible at all times, as in Joust (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 20, "Joust").
  - Player-killing, and challenge matches arranged in advance (Bartle 1996, "A Simple Taxonomy" and "Killers v. Killers").
  - A title other players can take from you, like a Foursquare mayorship (McGonigal 2011, ch. 8).
  - Yee's *Competition* items: "Challenging Others, Provocation, Domination" (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 5).
- **Example games:** Chess and sports (Caillois, as summarized in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 22, "Ludic Activities"); Quake, which the MDA paper credits with competition (Hunicke et al. 2004); StarCraft, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, DotA 2, Street Fighter, FIFA (Yee 2015).

### Progress, completion, and power

Collecting, leveling, rewards.

- **Named by:** Yee 2006 *Advancement*; Quantic Foundry *Completion* and *Power*; Schell 2019 *Completion* (p. 136); the Hallfords' four reward types, glory, sustenance, access, and facility, as given in Salen and Zimmerman 2003 (ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules"); Marczewski 2015 *Player*.
- **Aesthetic:** None of MDA's eight.
- **Dynamics:**
  - Goals within goals: short-term goals "generate pleasure through both of these functions: making plans as well as achieving them" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Goals Within Goals").
  - Reward schedules: rewards that arrive after a fixed or variable number of actions, or after a fixed or variable stretch of time (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules").
  - A climb in which "the more points you earn, the higher your level," and each level unlocks more challenging work (McGonigal 2011, ch. 3).
  - A "steady stream of incremental rewards" that forms "a tight loop of desire" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Meaningful Pleasure").
- **Mechanics:**
  - Points and levels (Bartle 1996, "A Simple Taxonomy"); leveling up and completing quests (Schell 2019, p. 552).
  - The Hallfords' four reward types: glory, which has no effect on play; sustenance, which lets the avatar keep what it has gained; access, to new places and resources; and facility, new or stronger abilities (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules").
  - "Collect all the treasures" and "clear the level" goals (Schell 2019, p. 136); every mission, collectible, and hidden location (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 11).
  - Collectibles with real value, as when every hundred rings in Sonic give an extra life (Schell 2019, p. 44).
  - New powers as rewards (Schell 2019, p. 232), and rewards that grow as the player progresses (p. 233).
  - Stat pop-ups like "+1 stamina," and visibly better gear (McGonigal 2011, ch. 3).
  - Leveling fast, acquiring rare items, and accumulating resources (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 11).
  - Points, prizes, unlocks, and visible status markers (Marczewski n.d., Player).
  - A caution: points, badges, and rewards added to an activity can drain the motivation it already had (Schell 2019, p. 158).
- **Example games:** World of Warcraft, Diablo for *Power*, and Final Fantasy IX, Pokémon, Assassin's Creed for *Completion* (Yee 2015); Pokémon gym medals and Ultima Online's player-set goals as short-term goals (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Goals Within Goals"); Half-Life's pacing of rewards (same chapter, "Rewards and Schedules").

### Discovery, curiosity, and novelty

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Discovery* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Bartle 1996 *Explorer*; Lazzaro 2004a *Easy Fun*; Schell 2019, Lens of Curiosity (p. 41) and Lens of Novelty (pp. 160 to 161); Malone 1980 *curiosity*; Quantic Foundry *Discovery*.
- **Aesthetic:** Discovery, "game as uncharted territory" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Hidden information revealed bit by bit, which "seems to provoke curiosity" (Malone 1980, p. 67), as in scouting through the fog of war, where "the strategic unveiling of hidden information adds suspense and tension" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 17, "Hiding and Revealing Systems").
  - A "rhythm of discovery" as collected coins unlock new worlds and powers in Super Mario 64 (same section).
  - Sandbox experiments: "What happens if I do this?" (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 1d).
  - Ambiguity, incompleteness, and detail that "create a living world" (Lazzaro 2004a, p. 4).
  - Surprising feedback (Malone 1980, p. 69).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Secrets to find and areas to explore completely (Koster 2013, p. 76); hidden secrets and treasures, and objects to experiment with (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 17).
  - Something new on each level (Schell 2019, p. 160).
  - Rewards that move the player to new parts of the game (Schell 2019, p. 232), like the Hallfords' access rewards.
  - Well-timed hints, which "renew their hope and their curiosity" (Schell 2019, p. 263).
  - A world to map and physics to probe (Bartle 1996, "A Simple Taxonomy"); a crafting system to test, as in Minecraft (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 13).
  - Exploring every zone, and finding quests, characters, and places few players know (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 11).
  - Exploration mechanics and unlockable content (Marczewski n.d., mechanics grid).
- **Example games:** Portal (Schell 2019, p. 160); Myst, EverQuest, Grand Theft Auto III (Lazzaro 2004a); BioShock and The World Ends with You as "discovery work" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1); The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, Minecraft, Kerbal Space Program (Yee 2015).

### Fantasy, role-play, and story

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Fantasy* and *Narrative* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Caillois 1961 *mimicry*; Yee 2006 *Role-Playing*; Malone 1980 *fantasy*; Quantic Foundry *Fantasy* and *Story*; Koster 2013 *storytelling* (p. 100).
- **Aesthetic:** Fantasy, "game as make-believe," and Narrative, "game as drama" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Dramatic tension, from "a rising tension, a release, and a denouement" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
  - Intrinsic fantasy, where the skill being practiced belongs to the fiction; Malone proposed that such fantasies are "both (a) more interesting and (b) more instructional" than fantasies laid on top (Malone 1980, p. 58).
  - Story that gives other mechanics a reason, as Jak and Daxter's plot gives Jak "a reason for collecting" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 26, "Two Structures for Narrative Play").
- **Mechanics:**
  - Levels that each present "a new piece of the story" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 4).
  - Alliances with non-player characters, formed and broken to shape the story (Przybylski et al. 2010, p. 156).
  - Invulnerability for most of a short pirate game, because "drama is part of the pirate fantasy" (Schell 2019, p. 66).
  - A choice among several fantasies, or names the player gives to imaginary participants (Malone 1980, p. 60).
  - Elaborate storylines and characters with back-stories (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 12).
  - Role-playing a character and trying out new roles (Yee 2006, manuscript pp. 11 to 12).
  - An avatar that represents the player in a shared fictional space (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure"), and an idealized avatar (Schell 2019, p. 374).
- **Example games:** Final Fantasy (Hunicke et al. 2004); Dragon Age: Inquisition, for the emotional relationships between its characters (Schell 2019, p. 128); Dragon Age, Mass Effect, Skyrim, Knights of the Old Republic, The Last of Us, Persona 4 (Quantic Foundry reference sheet); Dear Esther, Proteus, and Gone Home, walking simulators that remove the pressure of challenge (Juul 2019, pp. 190 to 191); masks and theater (Caillois, as summarized in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 22, "Ludic Activities").

### Expression, creativity, and construction

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Expression* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Yee 2006 *Customization*; Quantic Foundry *Design*; Radoff 2021, creating order out of chaos and customizing virtual worlds; Malone and Lepper 1987 *control*; Marczewski 2015 *Free Spirit*; self-determination theory's *autonomy* (Ryan et al. 2006), which runs across several rows (see the crosswalk).
- **Aesthetic:** Expression, "game as self-discovery" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Leaving a mark: expression "comes from dynamics that encourage individual users to leave their mark" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
  - Goals the players write themselves, as in Ultima Online, where "players can author their own experiences" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Goals Within Goals").
  - Status among creators, once veterans get content tools: "can they become the most popular and respected designer?" (Schell 2019, p. 451).
- **Mechanics:**
  - "Systems for purchasing, building or earning game items, for designing, constructing and changing levels or worlds, and for creating personalized, unique characters" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
  - Tools to design characters and to build and share levels (Schell 2019, p. 134), especially beside an online community (p. 155).
  - Clothing and decoration rewards, which "satisfy a basic urge to make a mark on the world" (Schell 2019, p. 232), and vanity items (p. 449).
  - Character creation, and customizing a city or spaceship with the tools and assets to do it (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 13).
  - Collecting building materials with friends, then creating levels for other players, as in Little Big Planet (McGonigal 2011, ch. 13).
  - Choosing resources before play, such as a Warhammer army or a Magic deck (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 28, "A Metagame Model").
  - Creativity tools and sandbox spaces; the site warns that color themes alone do not count (Marczewski n.d., Free Spirit).
  - Customizing a character at creation, and outfits that match in color and style (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 12).
- **Example games:** The Sims (Hunicke et al. 2004; McGonigal 2011, ch. 1; Yee 2015); Minecraft, where building serves both safe shelter and creativity (Schell 2019, p. 155); SingStar, and Madden NFL for "building and managing an online franchise," as "creative work" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1); Spore's shared player-made creatures (McGonigal 2011, ch. 13); Animal Crossing, Guild Wars 2 (Yee 2015).

### Fellowship and social connection

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Fellowship* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Bartle 1996 *Socialiser*; Lazzaro 2004a *The People Factor*; self-determination theory's *relatedness* (Ryan et al. 2006); McGonigal 2011, social connection (ch. 2); Yee 2006 *Social*; Quantic Foundry *Community*; Schell 2019, collaboration and meeting up (p. 439).
- **Aesthetic:** Fellowship, "game as social framework" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Information shared within a team, and winning conditions "more difficult to achieve alone" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3); tasks no one can do alone, since "collaborating and succeeding as a team is a special pleasure that can create lasting social bonds" (Schell 2019, p. 229).
  - Interdependence: classes or professions that need one another (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 4c), or healing that works only on other players, as in Toontown (Schell 2019, p. 129).
  - Reciprocity: seeing that a neighbor helped your farm gives "the urge to reciprocate" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 5).
  - Ambient sociability, playing alone in a shared world (McGonigal 2011, ch. 5).
  - Mentoring, from replaying Braid to coach friends and family (McGonigal 2011, ch. 5) to rewards for helping newcomers (Schell 2019, p. 450).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Friends lists (Schell 2019, pp. 129, 447); guild chat channels and voice chat (Przybylski et al. 2010, p. 156).
  - Asynchronous turns, which McGonigal calls the secret of Lexulous's pull (McGonigal 2011, ch. 5).
  - Short-term mission groups and long-term guilds or clans (Przybylski et al. 2010, p. 156).
  - Cooperative and competitive modes in one game, and same-room play for two to four people (Lazzaro 2004a, p. 5).
  - Property a group owns together, such as a ship (Schell 2019, p. 448), and scheduled community events (p. 453).
  - Saves: in Rock Band, a bandmate can revive a player who fails, so "one member's failure pushes the others to do better" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 4).
  - Teams, collaboration tools, and visible community (Marczewski n.d., Socialiser).
  - Playing grouped rather than solo (Yee 2006, manuscript p. 11).
- **Example games:** World of Warcraft raids and Castle Crashers as "teamwork" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1); Lexulous, FarmVille, Rock Band, and Braid replayed to coach friends and family (McGonigal 2011, ch. 5); Mario Kart, Dark Age of Camelot (Lazzaro 2004a); Charades (Hunicke et al. 2004); chess, tennis, League of Legends, Call of Duty, and Words with Friends as weekly games that hold friendships together (Schell 2019, p. 439); Portal 2 played with a friend, Final Fantasy XIV, Destiny (Quantic Foundry reference sheet).

### Sensation, thrill, and destruction

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Sensation* (Hunicke et al. 2004); Caillois 1961 *ilinx*; Schell 2019 *Thrill*, "fear minus death equals fun" (p. 137); Koster 2013 *visceral reactions* (p. 90); Apter's *facing danger*, as given in Salen and Zimmerman 2003 (ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure"); Quantic Foundry *Excitement* and *Destruction*.
- **Aesthetic:** Sensation, "game as sense-pleasure" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2); the paper names no dynamics for it.
- **Dynamics:**
  - Escalation: invaders that speed up as you destroy them (Schell 2019, p. 56), or missiles raining down until you lose (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "The Role of the Goal").
  - Threat on an unpredictable schedule, as in Half-Life, where "deadly threats seem to lurk in every dark shadow" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules").
  - The vertigo of moving through 3D space in real time (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure").
  - Risk against reward: "Taking risks is exciting" (Schell 2019, p. 235), as in choosing whether to play it safe or take a big risk (pp. 222 to 223).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Guns, explosions, gore, and destructible environments (Quantic Foundry reference sheet, p. 15), and tools to "blow things up" (p. 8).
  - Destruction on a scale real life cannot allow (Schell 2019, p. 128).
  - Tactile components, like Axis & Allies' plastic figures (Schell 2019, p. 134).
  - Physical input, as in Wii Boxing and Dance Dance Revolution (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1).
  - Animation that adds urgency, like Bookworm's burning letters (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 1b).
  - Player-versus-player combat, which "can be exciting" but can also make players feel "constantly threatened" (Schell 2019, p. 454).
  - A caution: graphic violence raised a game's appeal "only for those relatively high in aggression" (Przybylski et al. 2010, p. 159).
- **Example games:** Axis & Allies in Greg Costikyan's story about sensation (Schell 2019, p. 134); the vertigo of an Unreal deathmatch (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure"); Wii Boxing and Dance Dance Revolution as "physical work" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1); Grand Theft Auto V, Battlefield, Doom, Halo (Yee 2015); a child whirling until he falls, leapfrog, and waltzing (Caillois, as summarized in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 22, "Ludic Activities"); roller coasters (Schell 2019, p. 137).

### Chance

- **Named by:** Caillois 1961 *alea*; variable-ratio reward schedules in Salen and Zimmerman 2003 (ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules"); randomness as a way to make the outcome uncertain (Malone 1980).
- **Aesthetic:** None of MDA's eight, though the paper charts the odds of two six-sided dice to show how a mechanic shapes chance (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 3).
- **Dynamics:**
  - Surprise: "chance means uncertainty, and uncertainty means surprises" (Schell 2019, p. 193).
  - Variable-ratio reinforcement, the slot machine's schedule: "The repeat play of gamblers is strong evidence of the power of variable reinforcement" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules").
  - Reversals of fortune, as the chutes and ladders of Chutes and Ladders produce (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 15, "Chance and Game Play").
  - Chance alternating with skill, "an alternating pattern of tension and relaxation" (Schell 2019, p. 225).
  - Pushing your luck, as in the dice game Pig, "astonishingly simple, strategically deep, and increasingly dramatic" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 15, "Pig").
- **Mechanics:**
  - Dice and random card deals (Malone 1980, p. 52), and randomness used "to heighten interest" (p. 67).
  - Variable rewards: a one-in-three chance of thirty points "stays rewarding for a much longer time" than ten points every time, though the average is the same (Schell 2019, p. 233).
  - Choosing lottery numbers, which lets players "keep hope alive" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 15, "Chance and Game Play").
  - A caution: Lazzaro's challenge-seeking players prefer "strategy rather than luck" (Lazzaro 2004a, p. 3).
- **Example games:** Dice and roulette (Caillois, as summarized in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 22, "Ludic Activities"); gambling, racetracks, casinos, and lotteries (Caillois, quoted in Henricks 2010, p. 166); slot machines, and Half-Life's unpredictable monster attacks as "variable ratio punishments" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Rewards and Schedules").

### Submission, relaxation, and escape

- **Named by:** LeBlanc *Submission*, "game as pastime" in Hunicke et al. 2004 and "game as masochism" in Salen and Zimmerman 2003; Lazzaro 2004a *Altered States*; Koster 2013 *comfort* and *meditation* (p. 100); Yee 2006 *Escapism*; the recovery studies (Reinecke 2009; Koçak et al. 2024).
- **Aesthetic:** Submission, "game as pastime" (Hunicke et al. 2004, p. 2); the paper names no dynamics for it.
- **Dynamics:**
  - Rhythmic repetition, "the meditative patterns of Tetris" (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Patterns of Pleasure").
  - The ritual of rule-based play, as in Bejeweled and Solitaire (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure").
  - Comfort: playing where "one can exercise mastery with little risk" (Koster 2013, p. 100).
  - Busywork that keeps "our hands and mind occupied" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 1).
- **Mechanics:**
  - Lower difficulty settings, which players choose "when they want to relax" (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 3f).
  - Turn-based play, and a move counter in place of a clock (Lazzaro 2004b, sec. 1c).
  - Simple rules, which are "less work for our brain" (Schell 2019, p. 143).
  - Short casual-game breaks (McGonigal 2011, ch. 3).
  - A level to clear: "Clearing my mind by clearing a level" (Lazzaro 2004a, p. 4).
- **Example games:** Bejeweled, Solitaire (Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24, "Typologies of Pleasure"); Collapse, Tetris (Lazzaro 2004a); Minesweeper and Peggle as work breaks that leave executives "less stressed out" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 3); The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, Skyrim, Red Dead Redemption (Anto et al. 2024).

### Meaning and epic scale

- **Named by:** McGonigal 2011 *meaning* (ch. 2); Schell 2019 *Wonder* (p. 137); Marczewski 2015 *Philanthropist*.
- **Aesthetic:** None of MDA's eight.
- **Dynamics:**
  - Collective progress toward a vast goal: "pursuing a massive goal alongside millions of other people feels good. It feels meaningful" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 6).
  - Visible impact, as when World of Warcraft changes the world after a player's quests, so that "your actions are having a significant impact on the world" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 3).
- **Mechanics:**
  - A community-wide counter, like Halo 3's tally toward ten billion kills (McGonigal 2011, ch. 6).
  - A public service record of medals and achievements, "a history of a player's contributions to a larger organization" (McGonigal 2011, ch. 6).
  - Each player's points added to a chosen team's total, as in NCAA Football 10 (McGonigal 2011, ch. 6).
  - A running global total, like Free Rice's growing pile of donated rice (McGonigal 2011, ch. 11).
  - A public audience and regional "power meters," as in World Without Oil (McGonigal 2011, ch. 14).
  - Knowledge sharing, mentoring, and stewardship roles (Marczewski n.d., Philanthropist), though the site defines this type's purpose as altruism, not meaning in general.
- **Example games:** Halo 3's collective campaign to ten billion kills (McGonigal 2011, ch. 6); Free Rice and Foldit (McGonigal 2011, ch. 11); World Without Oil (McGonigal 2011, ch. 14).

## What the course books contribute

**Schell, *The Art of Game Design* (2019)** carries more of the frameworks
than any other course book. Chapter 9, "The Game Is Made for a Player,"
gives LeBlanc's eight pleasures (pp. 133 to 135), Bartle's four player
types (pp. 135 to 136) and Schell's own additions: anticipation, completion,
delight in another's misfortune (schadenfreude), gift giving, humor,
possibility, pride in an accomplishment (naches), surprise, thrill, triumph
over adversity (fiero) and wonder (pp. 136 to 137), gathered as Lens #20,
Pleasure. Chapter 11, "The Player's Mind Is Driven by the Player's Motivation," covers
Maslow's hierarchy with Minecraft as the worked example (pp. 154 to 156);
self-determination theory's competence, autonomy, and relatedness (pp. 155
to 156, Lens #22, Needs); intrinsic against extrinsic motivation, with the
question of whether Pac-Man's reward is the chase or the points (pp. 157 to
158); "wanna" against "hafta," with World of Warcraft guild pressure as the
cautionary case (pp. 158 to 160, Lens #23, Motivation); novelty (pp. 160 to
161, Lens #24); and judgment (p. 162, Lens #25). Chapter 24, "Some Games Are
Played with Other Players," gives five reasons we play with others:
competition, collaboration, meeting up, exploring our friends, and exploring
ourselves (pp. 438 to 441). Chapter 9's discussion of pleasures associated
with gender (pp. 128 to 130) is where Dragon Age: Inquisition, Barbie
Fashion Designer, the Sims games, Toontown Online, and Words with Friends
appear.

**McGonigal, *Reality Is Broken* (2011)** proposes four intrinsic rewards:
satisfying work, the experience or hope of being successful, social
connection, and meaning (ch. 2). Chapter 1 sorts the hard work games offer
into seven kinds, with examples for each: high-stakes work (Gran Turismo,
Left 4 Dead), busywork (Bejeweled, FarmVille), mental work (Brain Age, Age
of Empires), physical work (Wii Boxing, Dance Dance Revolution), discovery
work (BioShock, The World Ends with You), teamwork (World of Warcraft raids,
Castle Crashers) and creative work (The Sims, SingStar, Madden NFL). Each
chapter of Part One builds its argument on one or two games: Tetris and
Portal for unnecessary obstacles (ch. 1), Breakout for flow and fiero
(ch. 2), World of Warcraft for "blissful productivity" (ch. 3), Super Monkey
Ball 2 and Rock Band 2 for fun failure and hope (ch. 4), Lexulous and
FarmVille for social connection (ch. 5), and Halo 3 for epic scale (ch. 6).

**Salen and Zimmerman, *Rules of Play* (2003)** presents Caillois's four
categories, agôn, alea, mimicry, and ilinx, and how he crosses them with
paidia, free improvised play, and ludus, rule-bound play, to chart ludic
activities on a grid (ch. 22, "Ludic Activities", where the first term is
spelled "paida"). Chapter 24, "Games as the
Play of Pleasure," applies all four to one Unreal deathmatch and restates
LeBlanc's eight pleasures, with Bejeweled and Solitaire as the examples of
Submission. Its version of the list is LeBlanc's earlier one, which glosses
Submission as "game as masochism," meaning the pleasure of submitting to a
system; the MDA paper's later gloss is "game as pastime." The same section,
"Typologies of Pleasure," adds Michael Apter's arousal types: exposure to
arousing stimulation, fiction and narrative, challenge, exploration,
negativism, cognitive synergy, and facing danger. The chapter goes on to flow
("Game Flow"); the "same-but-different" pleasure of repeated play, with
Quake, Breakout, tennis, and Charades ("Sculpting Desire" and "Patterns of
Pleasure"); goals within goals, with Pokémon and Ultima Online ("Goals
Within Goals"); and the conditioned pleasure of reward schedules, with Gabe
Newell on Half-Life ("Conditioned Pleasure" and "Rewards and Schedules").

**Koster, *A Theory of Fun for Game Design* (2013)** argues that fun is
pattern mastery: "with games, learning is the drug" (p. 40). He separates
fun from aesthetic appreciation, visceral reactions, and social status
signals, citing LeBlanc's eight pleasures and Lazzaro's four keys (p. 90);
names the social emotions schadenfreude, fiero, naches, and kvell (p. 92);
and adds four reasons to play other than fun: practice, meditation,
storytelling, and comfort (p. 100). He attaches no game titles to these
categories.

**Juul, *Handmade Pixels* (2019); Zimmerman, *The Rules We Break* (2022);
and Fields, *Distributed Game Development* (2010)** offer no framework of
their own. Juul quotes Brian Moriarty's claim that sublime art "elicits play
in the soul," its pleasure lying in having "no rules, no goal, no purpose"
(p. 190), and reads that tension as the motivation behind the walking simulators Dear
Esther, Proteus, and Gone Home (p. 191). Zimmerman calls emergent complexity
"a big part of why we play games" in the Eclipse exercise (p. 45). Fields
discusses motivating development teams, not players.

## Frameworks beyond the course books

**Bartle, 1996.** "Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds, Spades" sorts players of
multi-user dungeons (MUDs) by whether they prefer acting or interacting, and
the world or other players: Achievers, Explorers, Socialisers, and Killers.
Its examples are MUD systems themselves: it names TinyMUD, LPMUD, and MOO,
and refers to the first MUD only as "Trubshaw's 1978 game." Wikipedia has a
summary.

**Yee, 2006.** "Motivations for Play in Online Games" built forty survey
items from Bartle's types and earlier surveys, and factor-analyzed the
answers of about 3,000 players of EverQuest, Dark Age of Camelot, Ultima
Online, and Star Wars Galaxies. Three components, ten subcomponents:
Achievement (advancement, mechanics, competition), Social (socializing,
relationship, teamwork), and Immersion (discovery, role-playing,
customization, escapism). The finding that matters most: motivations do not
suppress each other, so a player can score high on achievement and social at
once, which Bartle's quadrants ruled out. Escapism was the best predictor of
problematic use.

**Quantic Foundry, 2015 onward.** The Gamer Motivation Model, by Nick Yee
and Nicolas Ducheneaut, has six clusters and twelve motivations: Action
(destruction, excitement), Social (competition, community), Mastery
(challenge, strategy), Achievement (completion, power), Immersion (fantasy,
story), and Creativity (design, discovery). The reference sheet gives example
games for each motivation. Yee's 2015 post on the most popular games by
motivation lists the games most favored by the top fifth of scorers on each
motivation, normalized against each game's overall popularity. A 2024 post
(Yee 2024) reports that the average Strategy score fell to the 33rd
percentile of its June 2015 baseline by April 2024, a change more than twice
the size of the next largest; the other motivations stayed stable or moved
slightly.

**Lazzaro, 2004.** "Why We Play Games: Four Keys to More Emotion Without
Story" came from watching 30 adults play their favorite games for 90 to 120
minutes, and interviewing 15 people who do not play. The four keys are Hard
Fun (emotion from meaningful challenges, strategies, and puzzles, including
fiero: Civilization, Halo, Tetris), Easy Fun (curiosity held by ambiguity,
incompleteness, and detail: Myst, EverQuest, Grand Theft Auto III), Altered
States (play that changes how players feel inside, "games as therapy":
Collapse, Tetris), and The People Factor (competition, cooperation,
performance, and spectacle: Mario Kart, Dark Age of Camelot). Her later
writing renames the last two Serious Fun and People Fun (Lazzaro n.d.). Her
claim: best-selling games create emotion in at least three of the four keys,
and her site adds that players alternate among the keys within a single
session. A longer conference version (Lazzaro 2004b), archived with its
audio, adds many of the design examples cited in the motivator sections.

**Self-determination theory, 2006 and 2010.** Ryan, Rigby, and Przybylski
(2006) tested competence, autonomy, and relatedness in four studies: Super
Mario 64; The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time against A Bug's Life; Super
Mario 64, Super Smash Bros., Star Fox 64, and San Francisco Rush; and a
survey of 730 members of an online gaming community, in which in-game
relatedness correlated strongly with Yee's social motive (r = .66).
Przybylski, Rigby, and Ryan (2010) add examples: Halo 3 matching players by
performance so the challenge stays right; a score aggregated across all of a
player's Xbox 360 games, and the cheering crowd of Guitar Hero, as feedback
on competence; Final Fantasy, The Legend of Zelda, and Adventure as autonomy;
World of Warcraft guilds as relatedness; and the Wii controller and the
instrument controllers of Rock Band and Guitar Hero as "mastery of
controls." The PENS questionnaire puts the model into practice (Center for
Self-Determination Theory n.d.). Wikipedia covers the theory.

**Hunicke, LeBlanc, and Zubek, 2004.** The MDA paper carries LeBlanc's eight
aesthetics with one-line glosses (sensation as sense-pleasure, fantasy as
make-believe, narrative as drama, challenge as obstacle course, fellowship
as social framework, discovery as uncharted territory, expression as
self-discovery, submission as pastime) and four worked examples: Charades
(fellowship, expression, challenge), Quake (challenge, sensation,
competition, fantasy), The Sims (discovery, fantasy, expression, narrative),
and Final Fantasy (fantasy, narrative, expression, discovery, challenge,
submission). Quake's list includes competition, which is not one of the
eight. The course assigns the paper in full, due September 28. Wikipedia has
a summary.

**Caillois, 1958 (English 1961).** *Man, Play and Games* gives agôn
(competition, as in chess and sports), alea (chance; Caillois takes the name
from the Latin for the game of dice), mimicry (make-believe, from masks to
theater), and ilinx (vertigo, as when a child whirls until he falls), as
summarized in Salen and Zimmerman (2003, ch. 22, "Ludic Activities").
Examples of all four can be placed "on a continuum between two opposite
poles": paidia, the principle of "diversion, turbulence, free improvisation,
and carefree gaiety," and ludus, which binds that play with "arbitrary,
imperative, and purposively tedious conventions" (Caillois, quoted in
Henricks 2010, p. 167). Henricks's appreciation quotes the text at length,
including its examples of chance (p. 166) and
vertigo: whirling dervishes, high-wire acrobats, and Mexican voladores
(p. 169).

**Malone, 1980 and 1981; Malone and Lepper, 1987.** *What Makes Things Fun
to Learn?* (Malone 1980) surveyed 65 elementary-school students and ran
experiments with variants of Breakout, played by 10 Stanford
undergraduates, and of Darts, a fraction-learning game, played by 80 fifth
graders. It proposed challenge, fantasy, and curiosity, the last split into
sensory and cognitive, and named randomness as one way to make a game's
outcome uncertain. Malone (1981) formalized the theory; Malone and Lepper
(1987) added control as an individual motivation, and cooperation,
competition, and recognition as interpersonal ones.

**Radoff, 2011.** Radoff's post "Game Player Motivations" (2011b) arranges
immersion, achievement, cooperation, and competition on two axes: from single
player to many players, and from quantitative rewards such as points and
leaderboards to qualitative ones. His book *Game On* (2011a) lists
forty-two things that are fun, from collecting and completion to nurturing
and being scared; he republished the list online in 2021. No game titles.

**Marczewski, 2015.** The Gamification User Types Hexad (Marczewski 2015,
pp. 65 to 80) names Achiever, Socialiser, Philanthropist, Free Spirit,
Player, and Disruptor; Tondello et al. (2016) built and validated a
questionnaire that measures the six types. It is a framework for gamifying
systems that are not games, and it names no game titles.

## What the survey data adds

Relaxation and stress relief barely appear in the design-era taxonomies,
where only MDA's submission and Lazzaro's altered states cover them. In the
recent surveys below they rank first or second among the reasons people
give for playing.

| Survey | Top reasons to play |
|---|---|
| ESA 2025a, *Essential Facts* (5,000 U.S. respondents; figures for players 18 and older) | pass the time or relax 68%, to have fun 62%, keep my mind sharp 35% |
| ESA 2025b, *Power of Play* (24,216 players aged 16 and older in 21 countries) | to have fun 66%, stress relief or relaxation 58%, to keep my mind sharp or exercise my brain 45% |
| Newzoo survey of U.S. players, 2021, as summarized by Byshonkov 2021 | relax or unwind 60%, fill free time 48% |

Studies of recovery from stress support the survey pattern. Reinecke
(2009), surveying 1,614 people, found that games "are systematically used
after exposure to stressful situations and strain." Koçak, Gorgievski, and
Bakker (2024) followed 65 employees across 502 daily observations and found
that evening play predicts next-morning recovery through psychological
detachment, and next-morning vigor through mastery. Anto et al. (2024),
surveying 609 postgraduate students, link open-world games to cognitive
escapism, relaxation, and well-being. Zhao et al. (2025) found in a study of
40 participants that intense games can aid recovery from mentally demanding
tasks, with the effect depending on the workload of the task before. The
Motivation to Play Scale (Holl et al. 2024) recovers ten factors: creativity
and exploration, escapism, competition, prestige, enjoyment, achievement,
socializing, boredom, aggression, and skill.

## Crosswalk

The grid shows which frameworks name each theme; the list after it gives
each framework's own term.

| Theme | Bartle | Yee | QF | Lazzaro | SDT | MDA | Caillois | Malone |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Progress, mastery, winning | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Beating other people | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Exploring, tinkering | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |   | ● |
| Being someone else, story |   | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Making, building, customizing |   | ● | ● |   | ● | ● | ● | ● |
| Togetherness, helping | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● | ● |   | ● |
| Thrill, sensation |   |   | ● | ● |   | ● | ● | ● |
| Chance |   |   |   |   |   |   | ● | ● |
| Relaxing, passing time |   | ● |   | ● |   | ● |   |   |

Key: Bartle 1996; Yee 2006; QF, Quantic Foundry; Lazzaro 2004a; SDT,
self-determination theory (Ryan et al. 2006); MDA, Hunicke et al. 2004;
Caillois 1961; Malone, Malone 1980 and Malone and Lepper 1987.

**Progress, mastery, winning.** Bartle: *Achiever*. Yee: *Achievement*.
Quantic Foundry: *Mastery* and *Achievement*. Lazzaro: *Hard Fun*.
Self-determination theory: *competence*. MDA: *Challenge*. Caillois:
*agôn*. Malone: *challenge*; Malone and Lepper: *recognition*. Every
framework names it.

**Beating other people.** Bartle: *Killer*. Yee: *Competition*. Quantic
Foundry: *Competition*. Lazzaro: *The People Factor*. Self-determination
theory: *competence*. MDA: *Challenge*. Caillois: *agôn*. Malone and
Lepper: *competition*. Every framework names it.

**Exploring, tinkering.** Bartle: *Explorer*. Yee: *Discovery*. Quantic
Foundry: *Discovery* and *Strategy*. Lazzaro: *Easy Fun*.
Self-determination theory: *autonomy*. MDA: *Discovery*. Malone:
*curiosity*. Caillois has no category for it.

**Being someone else, story.** Yee: *Role-Playing* and *Escapism*. Quantic
Foundry: *Fantasy* and *Story*. Lazzaro: *Easy Fun*. Self-determination
theory: *presence*, which it treats as an outcome of need satisfaction
rather than a motive. MDA: *Fantasy* and *Narrative*. Caillois: *mimicry*.
Malone: *fantasy*. Bartle has no type for it.

**Making, building, customizing.** Yee: *Customization*. Quantic Foundry:
*Design*. Self-determination theory: *autonomy*. MDA: *Expression*.
Caillois: *mimicry*. Malone and Lepper: *control*. Bartle and Lazzaro have
no term for it.

**Togetherness, helping.** Bartle: *Socialiser*. Yee: *Social*. Quantic
Foundry: *Community*. Lazzaro: *The People Factor*. Self-determination
theory: *relatedness*. MDA: *Fellowship*. Malone and Lepper: *cooperation*.
Caillois has no category for it.

**Thrill, sensation.** Quantic Foundry: *Excitement* and *Destruction*.
Lazzaro: *Altered States*. MDA: *Sensation*. Caillois: *ilinx*. Malone:
*sensory curiosity*. Bartle, Yee, and self-determination theory have no
term for it.

**Chance.** Caillois: *alea*. Malone: *randomness*. No other framework
names it.

**Relaxing, passing time.** Yee: *Escapism*. Lazzaro: *Altered States*.
MDA: *Submission*. Bartle, Quantic Foundry, self-determination theory,
Caillois, and Malone have no term for it.

Four observations for teaching. The achievement and competence cluster is
the most universal; every framework has it. Social motivation splits
everywhere into a cooperative half and an adversarial half, and Yee's data
showed the two coexist in one player. Immersion is the least stable term:
Yee bundled discovery, role-play, customization, and escapism under it,
Quantic Foundry later split fantasy and story from discovery and design, and
self-determination theory treats presence as an outcome of need
satisfaction rather than a motive.

Fourth, self-determination theory's three needs sit underneath the clusters
rather than beside them. Competence lines up with challenge and mastery,
and relatedness with fellowship, but autonomy has no single row. The theory
defines it as "a sense of volition or willingness when doing a task" (Ryan
et al. 2006, p. 346), so it describes how any activity feels rather than
which activity it is. The theory's own examples of autonomy are open
choices of goals in Final Fantasy, The Legend of Zelda, and Adventure (Przybylski et al. 2010,
p. 156). Marczewski's Free Spirit joins exploration and creativity under it
(Marczewski 2015), and Schell's World of Warcraft guild, pressing members to
play more than they want, shows it lost (Schell 2019, pp. 158 to 160).
Building, exploring, or competing can each satisfy or frustrate autonomy,
depending on whether the player chose to be there.

## Attribution

Every example game in this note is one the cited source names, attached to
the motivator it illustrates here. The sources attach games in three
different ways:

- **Designer-chosen illustrations:** Schell, McGonigal, Salen and
  Zimmerman, Lazzaro, the MDA paper, and the Quantic Foundry reference
  sheet.
- **Games used as experimental stimuli:** the studies by Ryan, Rigby,
  and Przybylski, and by Malone.
- **Statistical favorites of high scorers:** Yee's 2015 post on the most
  popular games by motivation.

Koster, Radoff, and Marczewski attach no titles to their categories. Rigby
and Ryan's book *Glued to Games* (2011) is often cited online with game
examples; those could not be checked against the text and are left out.

## Bibliography

**Finding the sources.** Search for a book in the library catalog by title
or ISBN; Schell is available in full through CLIO. A DOI link opens the
publisher's page for an article; if it asks you to pay, sign in through the
library first. Where an author or journal posts a free copy, the entry gives
that link too. Web pages were checked on October 2, 2026.

### Sources quoted inside the books above

These are known here only through the book that quotes them; the
bibliographic details come from that book's notes.

Apter, Michael J. 1991. "A Structural-Phenomenology of Play." In *Adult
Play: A Reversal Theory Approach*, edited by J. H. Kerr and Michael J.
Apter. Swets & Zeitlinger. Quoted in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24.

Hallford, Neal, with Jana Hallford. 2001. *Swords and Circuitry: A
Designer's Guide to Computer Role Playing Games*. Prima Publishing. Quoted
in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24.

LeBlanc, Marc. 2000. Presentation at the Game Developers Conference. The
source of the eight pleasures as given in Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24.

Moriarty, Brian. 2011. "An Apology for Roger Ebert." Presentation at the
Game Developers Conference, San Francisco, March 4, 2011. Quoted in Juul
2019, p. 190.

Newell, Gabe. 2000. Remarks at "Computer and Video Games Come of Age: A
National Conference to Explore the Current State of an Entertainment
Medium," Comparative Media Studies, MIT, February 10–11, 2000. Quoted in
Salen and Zimmerman 2003, ch. 24.
